summary: This document extends PCEP for Segment Routing with focus on SIDs and SR-Algorithms in traffic engineering. An SR-Algorithm sets the path computation algorithm. It updates RFC 8664 and RFC 9603.

plainLanguage.summary: Segment Routing labels do not all mean the same thing: one may point the way that a shortest-path calculation would, another along a policy the operator has defined. This document lets a controller and a router say which rule applies, both per label and for the path as a whole. It also lets the controller demand a particular rule, and fail cleanly if it cannot be met.

subtitle: How PCEP peers learn which routing algorithm each Segment Routing label belongs to, and how a path request can demand one.

tldr.problem: An SR-Algorithm says which path computation rule an interior routing protocol applies to a segment identifier. Without it in PCEP, a controller cannot ask for a path computed by a particular rule, and it cannot tell a backup controller which rule was used.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9933 adds an Algorithm field to the segment routing subobjects of the explicit and record route objects, a new SR-Algorithm TLV in the label switched path attributes object that states the constraint, and capability flags so that both ends agree to use them. It also adds metric types for delay, bandwidth and operator-defined values.
tldr.outcome: The document updates RFC 8664 and RFC 9603, registers TLV type 66 and the new metric types at IANA, and requires that the strict flag be honoured, so a controller that insists on a particular algorithm either gets it or gets a clear failure.

today: RFC 9933 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2026, and it has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 8664 and RFC 9603, and IANA has registered the SR-Algorithm TLV type 66, the new METRIC object types 22 to 25 and 128 to 255, the capability flags and two PCEP error values.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 5440 describes the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol for communication between a Path Computation Client and a Path Computation Element, or between a pair of Path Computation Elements. RFC 8664 and RFC 9603 specify PCEP extensions to support Segment Routing over MPLS and IPv6 data planes respectively.

This document specifies extensions to PCEP to enhance support for SR traffic engineering, focusing on the use of Segment Identifiers and SR-Algorithms. An SR-Algorithm associated with a SID defines the path computation algorithm used by IGPs.

There are three sets of extensions. First, mechanisms are introduced for PCEP peers to exchange information about the SR-Algorithm associated with each SID, by extending the SR-ERO, SR-RRO, SRv6-ERO and SRv6-RRO subobjects to carry an Algorithm field; this updates RFC 8664 and RFC 9603 to enable such encoding. Second, mechanisms are defined for signalling a specific SR-Algorithm as a constraint to the PCE for path computation, using a new SR-Algorithm TLV carried in the Label Switched Path Attributes object. Third, several new metric types are introduced for the METRIC object, to support optimization metrics derived from Flexible Algorithm Definitions during Flexible Algorithm path computation; their application is not restricted to Flexible Algorithms, and they may be used with label switched paths set up using different Path Setup Types.
sections.plainLanguage: PCEP is the protocol a router uses to ask a central controller for a path, and to have the controller install one. This document adds three things to that conversation: which algorithm each label in the path was computed with, a way to ask for a path computed with a named algorithm, and a way to express the delay and bandwidth numbers such an algorithm optimizes on.

sections.title: Motivation
sections.content:
Existing PCEP specifications lack mechanisms to explicitly signal and negotiate SR-Algorithm capabilities and constraints. This limits the ability of a controller to make informed path computation decisions based on the specific SR-Algorithms supported and desired within the network. The absence of an explicit SR-Algorithm specification in PCEP messages implied no specific constraint on the SR-Algorithm to be used, effectively allowing the use of SIDs with any SR-Algorithm.

A primary motivation is to enable the controller to use the path computation logic and topological information derived from IGPs, including Flexible Algorithms. Aligning controller path computation with these IGP algorithms lets operators obtain paths that are congruent with the underlying routing behaviour, which can result in segment lists with fewer SIDs, and support for SR-Algorithm constraints simplifies the deployment and management of Flexible Algorithm paths in multi-domain scenarios.

The controller and the client may independently compute SR traffic engineering paths with different SR-Algorithms, and that information needs to be exchanged between peers for network monitoring and troubleshooting. In scenarios involving multiple controllers, when a client receives a path from the primary controller it must be able to report the complete path information, including the SR-Algorithm, to a backup controller, which is essential for high availability, because the backup controller must be able to verify Prefix SIDs correctly.

The ability to specify an SR-Algorithm per SID is also needed for several reasons. Some SID types, such as Binding SIDs, may not have an SR-Algorithm specified, and it may be inaccurate to state that an entire end-to-end path adheres to a specific algorithm if it includes a Binding SID from another policy. And there may be topologies with two IGP domains, each using the same Flexible Algorithm Definition but with differing algorithm numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: Two reasons stand out. First, a controller that ignores the algorithm will compute a path that does not follow the same rules the interior routing protocol uses, so the traffic would not actually travel where the controller believes. Second, if a backup controller takes over, it has to be told which algorithm the labels in the installed path were computed with, or it cannot check them.

sections.title: Capability Flags
sections.content:
The SR-PCE-CAPABILITY sub-TLV is defined in Section 4.1.2 of RFC 8664 and is included in the PATH-SETUP-TYPE-CAPABILITY TLV. This document defines a flag in its Flags field: S, the SR-Algorithm Capability, at bit 5. If the S flag is set to 1, a PCEP speaker indicates support for the Algorithm field and the Subobject Extension Block in the SR-ERO subobject, and for the SR-Algorithm TLV, for label switched paths set up using Path Setup Type 1 for Segment Routing. It does not indicate support for these extensions for other Path Setup Types. If the flag is set to 0, behaviour reverts to the procedures defined in existing specifications.

The SRv6-PCE-CAPABILITY sub-TLV is defined in Section 4.1.1 of RFC 9603 and is included in the PATH-SETUP-TYPE-CAPABILITY TLV. This document defines the same S flag, the SR-Algorithm Capability, at bit 13, indicating support for the Algorithm field in the SRv6-ERO subobject and for the SR-Algorithm TLV for label switched paths set up using Path Setup Type 3 for SRv6.

The PCEP extensions defined in Sections 5.1 and 5.2 of the document must not be used unless both PCEP speakers have indicated support by setting the S flag in the Path Setup Type sub-TLV corresponding to the path setup type of the label switched path.
sections.plainLanguage: Before any of this is used, the two ends have to say that they understand it. Each declares a separate capability for the MPLS form of Segment Routing and for the IPv6 form, and both ends must set it. If either end has not, the extensions must not be used at all.

sections.title: The SR-Algorithm TLV
sections.content:
A new TLV for the LSPA object is introduced to carry the SR-Algorithm constraint. It must only be used when the path setup type is 1 for SR-MPLS or 3 for SRv6. Only the first instance of this TLV must be processed, and subsequent instances must be ignored.

The TLV has a 16-bit Type field with the value 66 and a 16-bit Length field with the value 4. The 32-bit value is formatted as 16 bits of reserved space that must be set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver, then 8 bits of flags, of which only one is defined, then the 8-bit algorithm field.

The S flag, for strict, says that the path computation at the controller must fail if the specified SR-Algorithm constraint cannot be satisfied. If the strict bit is unset and the controller is unable to compute a path that satisfies the constraint, it must attempt to compute a path as if no SR-Algorithm constraint had been requested, which means it may use any available SR-Algorithm, consistent with the default behaviour in the absence of a constraint.
sections.plainLanguage: The constraint travels in the part of the message that describes the requested path. It names one algorithm in a single byte, with numbers from 0 to 127 for the ordinary algorithms and 128 to 255 for the Flexible Algorithms. The strict flag decides what happens when the controller cannot meet the request: with the flag set, the request fails; without it, the controller falls back to computing a path with whatever algorithm it has.

sections.title: New Metric Types
sections.content:
The METRIC object is defined in Section 7.8 of RFC 5440. This document specifies additional types for it, to enable the encoding of optimization metric types derived from the Flexible Algorithm Definition during Flexible Algorithm path computation. While these new metric types are defined to support that use case, their use is not restricted to Flexible Algorithm path computation or to any specific path setup type.

The types are T=22 for the Path Min Delay metric, T=23 for the P2MP Path Min Delay metric, T=24 for the Path Bandwidth metric, T=25 for the P2MP Path Bandwidth metric, and T=128 to 255 for a user-defined metric.

The Path Min Delay metric represents the sum of the minimum link delay of all links along a point-to-point path, where the minimum link delay of a link is the measured minimum delay over a configurable interval, and the delay is advertised in microseconds. The P2MP Path Min Delay metric encodes the value for the destination that observes the worst, that is highest, delay among all the destinations of the tree, so it is the maximum of the per-destination path values.

The Path Bandwidth metric represents the sum of the bandwidth metric of all links along a point-to-point path, and the P2MP Path Bandwidth metric again takes the worst of the per-destination values. The bandwidth metric of a link may be the original metric advertised on the link, which may have a value inversely proportional to the link capacity. The user-defined metric types are assigned by an operator for local use, and the range was chosen so that it maps onto values in the IGP Metric-Type registry, so that the user-defined metric type 130 in PCEP can represent the sum of user-defined metric 130 of all links along a path. All these values are encoded in IEEE floating point format.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the numbers a controller can optimize on. The delay metric adds up the delay of every link on the path, and the bandwidth metric adds up the bandwidth figures. For a tree with several destinations, the value reported is the worst of the per-destination values. The last range is left for operators to define their own numbers, chosen so that they line up with the metric types the routing protocols already use.

sections.title: The SR-Algorithm Constraint
sections.content:
To signal a specific SR-Algorithm constraint to the controller, the headend must encode the SR-Algorithm TLV inside the LSPA object. If a client receives an LSPA object with the TLV as part of a PCInitiate or PCUpd message, it must include an LSPA object with the TLV in a PCRpt message as part of the intended attribute list. If a controller receives an LSPA object with the TLV in a PCRpt or PCReq, it must include the LSPA object with the TLV in a PCUpd message, or a PCRep message in the case of an unsuccessful path computation. A peer that did not advertise the S flag must ignore the SR-Algorithm TLV on receipt.

The controller must not use Prefix SIDs associated with an SR-Algorithm other than the one specified in the constraint. If a protected Adjacency SID is used without an associated SR-Algorithm, there is a risk that the backup path fails to forward traffic over parts of the topology that are not included in the specified SR-Algorithm, so it is not recommended to use protected Adjacency SIDs without an explicitly specified SR-Algorithm. If an Adjacency SID has an associated SR-Algorithm, the controller must ensure that it matches the one specified in the constraint. Other SID types, such as Binding SIDs, are allowed, and a path Binding SID from another policy is permitted only if the path associated with that policy fully satisfies all the constraints of the current path computation.

The specified constraint is applied to the end-to-end path. Using different constraints, or a winning definition with different metrics or constraints for the same SR-Algorithm in each domain of a single computation, is out of scope. If the controller cannot find a path with the given constraint, does not support that combination of constraints, or the definition contains constraints, metrics or other attributes it does not support or recognize, it must use an empty ERO in PCInitiate for instantiation, a PCUpd message if an update is required, or a NO-PATH object in PCRep. If the algorithm value is in the range 128 to 255, the controller must perform path computation according to the Flexible Algorithm procedures; otherwise it must adhere to the path computation procedures with SID filtering. An SR-Algorithm does not replace the objective function defined in RFC 5541.
sections.plainLanguage: The constraint travels from the router to the controller in the request, and the router repeats it back in its report, so both sides keep a record of what was asked for. The controller then has to honour it: it may not build the path from labels that belong to a different algorithm. If it cannot find a path that satisfies the request, it says so with an empty path rather than returning something that quietly uses another algorithm.

sections.title: Path Computation for Flexible Algorithms
sections.content:
This section applies only to the Flexible Algorithms range of SR-Algorithm values. The controller performs Flexible Algorithm path computation based on topology information stored in its traffic engineering database, which is expected to be populated with the necessary information, including Flexible Algorithm Definitions, node participation and Application-Specific Link Attributes, through standard mechanisms such as IGPs with traffic engineering extensions or BGP Link State.

The controller must follow the IGP Flexible Algorithm path computation logic of RFC 9350. That includes performing the definition selection, determining the topology associated with a specific Flexible Algorithm, using node participation and Application-Specific Link Attributes, and applying the other rules for Flexible Algorithm path calculation. Those procedures are further extended by other documents such as RFC 9843, and the registry of ordered pruning rules created by RFC 9917 must also be used. The controller must optimize the computed path based on the metric type specified in the definition, and the optimization metric type included in PCEP messages from the client must be ignored. The controller must use the metric type from the definition in messages it sends to the client, unless that metric type is not defined in PCEP or not supported by the peer. It is allowed to use SID types other than Prefix SID, such as Adjacency or Binding SIDs, but only from nodes participating in the specified SR-Algorithm.

The controller must use the constraints specified in the definition and also constraints, except the optimization metric type, directly included in PCEP messages from the client. It may decide to ignore specific constraints received from the client based on existing processing rules, and if it does not support a specified combination of constraints it must fail path computation and respond with an empty ERO or a NO-PATH object. The client must not include constraints from the definition in the message it sends, and the controller should not include them in messages it sends back. Adding more constraints on top of those in the definition requires complex path computation and may reduce the benefit of the scheme, and may require a longer list of SIDs for the computed path.
sections.plainLanguage: For the Flexible Algorithm numbers, the controller works out the path the way the interior routing protocol would, using the same definition and the same rules, and it optimizes on the metric that the definition names. Whatever metric the client asked for is ignored, because the definition is what the network is actually running. The client should not repeat the definition's own constraints in the request, since the controller already knows them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security considerations described in RFC 5440, RFC 8231, RFC 8253, RFC 8281, RFC 8664, RFC 9603 and RFC 9350 apply to these extensions as well. The document notes that this specification introduces the possibility of computing paths by the controller based on Flexible-Algorithm-related topology attributes, and based on the metric type and constraints from the definition, which creates additional vulnerabilities of the kinds already described in the documents it builds on.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds no new security considerations of its own and follows the rules already set for PCEP and for Flexible Algorithms. It does note one new exposure: because the controller can now compute paths using the attributes and constraints of a Flexible Algorithm definition, the same kinds of problem that those mechanisms already have apply here too.

viz.caption: Why the algorithm has to be named

items.title: Binding SIDs
items.text: A binding SID may have no algorithm of its own, so claiming the whole path uses one algorithm could be wrong.

items.title: Two IGP domains
items.text: Two domains can use the same definition but different algorithm numbers.

items.title: High availability
items.text: A backup controller must be told the algorithm so that it can verify the prefix SIDs it is given.

items.title: Aligning with the IGP
items.text: Using the same rules as the interior routing protocol gives paths that match the routing and may need fewer labels.
